note.question: What determines a manufacturer’s optimal entry strategy in the product-sharing market and the economic implications of its entry?
note.overview: Mobile communications technologies and online platforms have enabled large-scale consumer-to-consumer (C2C) sharing of their underutilized products. This paper studies a manufacturer’s optimal entry strategy in the product-sharing market and the economic implications of its entry. Sharing of products or services among consumers has experienced dramatic growth in recent years.

source.quote: This paper studies a manufacturer’s optimal entry strategy in the product-sharing market and the economic implications of its entry.
In some situations, the manufacturer’s entry in the sharing market provides not only economic benefits to the firm and consumers, but also environmental benefits to the society as a whole.

In response to C2C product sharing, many manufacturers (e.g., General Motors and BMW) have entered the product-sharing market to provide business-to-consumer (B2C) rental services in addition to outright sales to consumers.

So, for analytical simplicity, we will consider the third-party sharing platform and the manufacturer’s own B2C sharing platform together as the “product-sharing market” for the purpose of determining an equilibrium rental price in the market.
Consider a market with a monopolist manufacturer producing a product at a constant marginal cost c and selling it at price p to consumers.
Note that a consumer’s usage value for a period represents how much the consumer beneﬁts from using the product in that period.

components.explanation: When the transaction cost for consumer-toconsumer sharing is low and the manufacturer’s marginal cost of production is not very high, the manufacturer will find it optimal not to offer its own rental service.

components.formal: Objective relation: When the transaction cost for consumer-toconsumer sharing is low and the manufacturer’s marginal cost of production is not very high, the manufacturer will find it optimal not to offer its own rental service.
conditions: If the manufacturer sells the product in the retail market (i.e., D(p, q) > 0), it will find it optimal to not offer the rental service in the first period (during which consumers make purchases).

When D(p, q) > 0, the manufacturer’s profit function includes three terms: the manufacturer’s revenue at the primary retail market, the manufacturer’s rental revenue from the sharing market, and the manufacturer’s total production cost.

When D(p, q) = 0—that is, no consumers buy the product (due to too high a price)—consumers can still rent the product from the manufacturer, in which case the manufacturer’s profit function includes two terms: the manufacturer’s rental revenue from the sharing market and its total production cost.
